lead: Body tracking and hand tracking turn a person's motion into numbers a computer can use. Sensors measure points on the body or hand; a skeleton model is fitted to those points; the fitted joint angles drive an avatar or an animation. Motion capture is the recording side of the same idea: it stores the motion for replay. The work appears in film and game animation, live sports analysis, VR avatars, and clinical biomechanics. Some syllabi call this movement capture or video-based input.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.2 for tracker coordinates and Chapter 2.4 for glove sensing; Unit 4 covers the kinematic chain and joint hierarchy.

blocks.text: A tracked body is a joint hierarchy: a root at the pelvis, then spine, neck, head, arms and legs, each joint a parent of the next. The hierarchy gives a compact state: joint angles plus the root position and orientation (6 degrees of freedom for the root). A T-pose calibration records each marker's offset from its bone while the actor stands with arms out. These offsets form the rest pose. During a take, cameras triangulate marker positions. Forward kinematics computes joint positions from angles; inverse kinematics solves the reverse, finding angles that place joints so markers match measurement. Occlusion happens when a body part hides a marker from a camera; the solver must bridge the gap. The capture volume is the space seen by enough cameras at once.

items: Place 40 reflective markers on bony landmarks.
Record a T-pose; store each marker offset in its bone frame.
Triangulate each marker from at least two camera views.
Fit the skeleton by inverse kinematics to the measured points.
Write joint angles per frame; fill gaps where markers were hidden.

blocks.text: Motion capture systems differ in what they measure and what they cost to clean. Passive optical systems use retro-reflective markers that bounce camera light back; active optical systems use LEDs that blink in patterns; markerless systems use video and image features; magnetic systems measure a field; mechanical exoskeletons measure joint angles directly; inertial suits integrate accelerometers and gyroscopes. Table 1 compares the families on the quantities that decide a shoot.

sections.h3: Hand tracking and where it is used

blocks.text: A hand model commonly has 21 joints: the wrist plus four joints for each finger. Camera-based hand tracking estimates these joints from images. Fingers occlude each other: from one view a bent finger can hide the next finger, and depth is ambiguous. A data glove (see Chapter 2.4) measures bend directly and avoids this, but it needs wiring and calibration. In a VR headset, hand tracking must run on limited power, so it uses lower resolution and predicts missing joints. Body and hand capture feed animation, live performance, sports biomechanics, VR avatars, and face capture.

items: Animation: retarget joint angles to a character.
Live performance: drive an avatar on set.
Sports: measure joint angles and timing.
VR: map headset cameras to hand joints for input.

figure.caption: Markers on the suit are seen by the camera ring, triangulated into 3D points, then fitted by inverse kinematics to give joint angles. The worked example's 10 s take holds 48,000 marker samples (576 kB raw), and the 300 samples lost to occlusion must be bridged by the solver.

spec.title: Optical capture: the 10 s take
spec.aria: Pipeline from 40 reflective markers on the suit through 12 cameras at 120 frames per second and triangulation into 48,000 samples, then inverse kinematics fitting the skeleton to output joint angles, with 300 occlusion-lost samples bridged into the fit.

examples.question: An optical motion capture stage uses 12 cameras at 120 frames per second and 40 markers on the actor. A 10-second take is recorded. (a) How many marker samples are there? (b) Each sample is three coordinates stored as 4-byte floats; what is the raw data size? (c) The actor turns and 5 markers are hidden from all cameras for 0.5 s; how many marker samples are lost?
steps: (a) Marker samples = markers × frames per second × seconds = 40 × 120 × 10 = 48,000 marker samples.
(b) Coordinates = 48,000 × 3 = 144,000 coordinates. Raw bytes = 144,000 × 4 = 576,000 bytes, about 576 kB using 1 kB = 1000 bytes.
(c) Lost samples = lost markers × frames per second × lost time = 5 × 120 × 0.5 = 300 marker samples.
examples.answer: The take has 48,000 marker samples, raw data is 576,000 bytes (about 576 kB), and 300 marker samples are lost.
examples.check:
markers = 40
fps = 120
seconds = 10
samples = markers * fps * seconds
print(samples)
coordinates = samples * 3
raw_bytes = coordinates * 4
print(raw_bytes)
lost_markers = 5
lost_time = 0.5
lost_samples = lost_markers * fps * lost_time
print(int(lost_samples))

traps: Markers give positions, not joint angles; the skeleton fit is a separate step that produces angles.
A lost marker is not a lost limb: the solver interpolates across the gap and can invent motion that never happened.
A T-pose is a rest calibration pose, not an animation pose; mistaking it for the take corrupts the bone offsets.
More cameras increase capture volume and redundancy, but they do not automatically raise the frame rate.
Do not swap active and passive optical systems: active markers emit light, passive markers reflect camera light.

quiz.q: What is a T-pose calibration used for in body tracking?
quiz.a: It records each marker's offset from its bone in a known rest pose, so later marker positions can be mapped to the skeleton.

quiz.q: Why does a marker-based optical system need inverse kinematics after triangulation?
quiz.a: Triangulation gives 3D marker positions only. Inverse kinematics finds the joint angles that place the skeleton so its joints best match those measured points.

quiz.q: A passive optical stage has 30 markers and records at 60 frames per second. A 4 s take is stored. How many marker samples are stored?
quiz.a: Marker samples = 30 markers × 60 frames per second × 4 s = 7200 marker samples.

quiz.q: A marker is hidden for 0.25 s at 120 frames per second, and the solver interpolates across the gap. What can go wrong in the animation?
quiz.a: The solver can invent a smooth path that never happened, causing foot sliding, wrong hand contact, or a limb that passes through an object.

quiz.q: How many joints are in the common hand model, and how are they arranged?
quiz.a: 21 joints: the wrist plus four joints for each of the five fingers.

quiz.q: Give one reason a data glove can beat a camera for finger tracking and one reason a camera can beat a glove.
quiz.a: A glove measures finger bend directly and avoids finger-to-finger occlusion. A camera needs no worn hardware and does not need wiring or per-user calibration.

quiz.q: Why is clean-up cost high for markerless video capture?
quiz.a: There are no physical markers to identify points, so image features can be ambiguous, fingers and limbs occlude each other, and an artist must correct false matches and missing depth frame by frame.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer headsets use neural hand tracking from cameras and fuse it with inertial data. Research motion capture uses learned pose estimators that need less clean-up but can fail on unusual body shapes. Sports labs combine optical capture with force plates. Search terms: markerless motion capture, pose estimation, inertial motion capture drift, hand pose estimation.
